_assertion_legend._comment: No automated runner ships yet. This classifies how each assertion should be verified by a future grader. manual-grep assertions have a concrete rule in _checks (a bundled script line or a file test); qualitative assertions need an LLM or human judge; mixed assertions start from a mechanical probe and end in judgment.

_checks.scaffold_index_first_selfcheck_last: index.html exists and bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/tech-tutorial/scripts/verify_structure.sh" <dir> -> PASS  self-check naming + position
_checks.no_forbidden_voice_phrases: bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/tech-tutorial/scripts/verify_prose.sh" <dir> -> PASS  forbidden voice phrases (English output only)
_checks.sections_are_h2_not_separate_files: index.html has >=3 <h2> sections and no NN-*.html siblings
_checks.no_separate_chapter_files: no NN-*.html files next to index.html
_checks.output_is_markdown: output is .md files and no .html files
_checks.related_tutorials_block_present: the new index.html has <section class="related-tutorials"> whose local links resolve
_checks.hub_index_updated_with_new_card: the hub index.html has a .tutorial-cards link to the new tutorial's index.html
_checks.prose_gates_pass: bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/tech-tutorial/scripts/verify_prose.sh" <dir> exits 0; any EXEMPT lines are justified in the delivery note

_qualitative_checks._comment: These rubrics apply to cases 17-20. Judge meaning and usable reader behavior, not exact wording. A listed assertion passes only when its semantic requirements hold; a material contradiction or omission fails it. No behavioral baseline or candidate output has been measured merely by adding these cases.
_qualitative_checks.chinese_ste_adaptation_has_no_compliance: Uses clear Chinese as an adaptation of STE principles. Fails if it claims formal Chinese ASD-STE100 compliance, converts English word limits into a Chinese character limit, or imposes an unsupported fixed character cap.
_qualitative_checks.preserves_causal_chain_and_boundaries: Explains the supplied cause, intervening mechanism, result, and applicable boundary without replacing them with slogans or unexplained labels. Fails if simplification changes why the result occurs or extends a guarantee beyond its stated conditions.
_qualitative_checks.preserves_modality_conditions_and_uncert: Preserves permission versus obligation, every material prerequisite, version scope, conditional benefit, and unverified status. Fails if may becomes must or will, an optional action becomes mandatory, or an unverified result becomes a confirmed claim.
_qualitative_checks.preserves_temporal_and_parallel_relation: Keeps only-after as a prerequisite and preserves actions that occur concurrently. Fails if sequencing words reverse the dependency or turn simultaneous actions into consecutive steps.
_qualitative_checks.procedure_establishes_environment_and_wo: Names the supplied shell/runtime assumptions, establishes a working directory, creates needed inputs, and makes relative paths resolvable from the stated location. Fails if a reader starting elsewhere must guess setup, file contents, or the command's working directory.
_qualitative_checks.actions_have_observable_results_and_wron: Pairs material actions with a visible result or a concrete verification command, identifies what the reader should notice, and gives an actionable check for a plausible failure. Fails if success is asserted without something observable or troubleshooting only says to try again.
_qualitative_checks.distinguishes_expected_from_observed_res: Clearly presents unexecuted commands and their results as expected, and states that execution was not performed. Fails if it invents terminal output, screenshots, successful tests, or observed files from an unrun procedure.
_qualitative_checks.adapts_scaffolding_without_removing_mech: Gives novices a concrete worked situation and defined terms; lets experts reach the mechanism and tradeoffs directly. Both versions preserve the supplied mechanism, conditions, and failure boundary. Fails if the versions differ only in length or the easier version loses a material condition.
_qualitative_checks.keeps_necessary_established_technical_te: Uses the domain's established terms consistently and explains unfamiliar ones for the declared reader. Fails if technical terms are rejected merely because they are absent from a controlled-language dictionary, replaced by invented labels, or removed along with the concept they name.

evals.name: open-ended-web-framework
evals.prompt: I want to learn a Python web framework systematically. I have only written small scripts and a few Flask routes. Write a tutorial that builds a complete mental model.
evals.expected_output: An English concept-focused tutorial. The structure follows the scaffold rather than a fixed chapter count: index first, *-self-check last, topical chapters in between based on the concept dependency graph. It scopes the topic to core concepts instead of the whole ecosystem. It uses the reader's Flask/script background as the starting analogy, includes scenario walkthroughs, has tradeoff tables, contains at least three cross-chapter discrimination questions, uses a learning-path breadcrumb, and avoids cheerleading or first-person author narration.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: a docs-paraphrase page organized by API surface, no concept map, no background calibration, no discrimination questions, no learning-path breadcrumb, and casual 'let's' style.

evals.name: scoped-database-indexes
evals.prompt: I need to optimize a slow business query. Teach me the parts of PostgreSQL indexes and query plans that I need for diagnosis. Do not cover the whole database kernel.
evals.expected_output: The tutorial stays scoped to indexes and query planning. It covers index types, selectivity, execution plans, misestimation, hello-world and realistic examples, component-level tradeoffs, concrete pitfalls, and runnable SQL when possible.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: an index-type reference page and EXPLAIN syntax list, broad database overview creep, no progressive examples, no tradeoffs, no concrete pitfalls.

evals.name: feature-deep-dive
evals.prompt: I do not understand why PKCE exists in OAuth 2.0. The docs show configuration steps but not the reason. Teach me PKCE properly: a short tutorial I can study, not just an answer.
evals.expected_output: The tutorial centers on why, not configuration. It compares the older authorization-code flow, explains authorization-code interception, public-client secrets, mobile threat models, limitations, when not to use it, and includes a protocol flow diagram.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: a PKCE setup how-to that stops at the API surface and omits design motivation, old-flow comparison, and protocol diagram.

evals.name: no-invented-terminology
evals.prompt: Teach me JavaScript's event loop, microtasks, macrotasks, and execution ordering. I have written JS for years but still cannot predict scheduling reliably.
evals.expected_output: A concept-focused English tutorial using community terms: event loop, microtask, macrotask, call stack, task queue. It does not invent labels such as 'task pump' or 'three-state scheduler'. The core idea is a sentence using standard terms. Reader prose does not leak cognitive-science jargon. It includes execution-order diagrams and at least three scheduling prediction questions.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: coined labels, pedagogy jargon in reader prose, and no execution-order discrimination questions.

evals.name: depth-and-frontier-fast-moving
evals.prompt: I want to understand LLM inference optimization: KV cache, PagedAttention, continuous batching, and speculative decoding. I can tune vLLM flags but do not understand the mechanisms or current frontier.
evals.expected_output: A deep concept-focused tutorial. It explains mechanisms one level below docs, such as how PagedAttention manages KV cache like virtual memory pages and why reduced fragmentation improves throughput. It includes dated field-state framing in index.html, distinguishes stable from fast-changing techniques, names superseded approaches, uses recent primary sources, and includes at least three cross-concept 'which technique fits this scenario?' discrimination questions.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: surface restatements such as 'PagedAttention improves throughput', no dated field-state note, and outdated secondary sources.

evals.name: broad-topical-concept-structure
evals.prompt: I want to understand Kafka systematically: log storage, partitions, replicas and ISR, consumer groups and rebalance, and exactly-once semantics. Build a full mental model with tradeoffs.
evals.expected_output: A broad concept-focused tutorial with more than four files when the dependency graph requires it. It uses 01-concepts and 02-principles as anchors, then subject-named topical chapters such as 03-storage-log, 04-replication, and 05-consumer-groups. It may include a frontier chapter for KRaft replacing ZooKeeper. index.html has audience sections, dated field-state framing, and a core-idea sentence. The self-check is last and includes at least three cross-chapter discrimination questions. Every chapter has a figure.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: forced four-file shape, generic chapter names such as 03-extra, no dependency-graph decomposition, no frontier framing, and missing audience routing.

evals.name: hands-on-mode-regression
evals.prompt: I want to learn FastAPI by building a small local service with dependency injection, Pydantic validation, and async routes. Give me a code progression I can run.
evals.expected_output: Hands-on mode. It contains a worked -> partial -> open practice chapter, a concrete pitfalls chapter, a capstone with discrimination decisions, and a final self-check. Code is runnable or marked unverified. Every chapter has a figure. Prose avoids cheerleading, first-person author narration, and casual slang.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: copied README snippets, no progression, no meaningful blanks, no capstone discrimination, and casual 'let's code' prose.

evals.name: library-hub-integration
evals.prompt: Add a multi-agent-patterns tutorial to my learning directory and connect it to the existing library. Update the homepage index and link related tutorials.
evals.expected_output: If the target directory already has sibling tutorials and a root hub, the output creates the new tutorial, updates the root hub incrementally under the appropriate theme cluster, preserves existing entries, and adds a Related tutorials block only for verified sibling paths.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: an isolated new tutorial folder with no hub update and no verified cross-links.

evals.name: markdown-fallback-mode
evals.prompt: Write an async/await tutorial for our GitHub wiki in Markdown. The wiki supports Mermaid and HTML details blocks.
evals.expected_output: Markdown output that preserves the cognitive structure: concept progression, worked-example order, diagrams in renderer-supported form, and retrieval separation through details blocks. It does not force standalone HTML or raw inline SVG when the host format does not support it.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: HTML template dumped into a wiki, or a prose-only Markdown page with diagrams and hidden answers removed.

evals.name: quick-primer-single-file
evals.prompt: Give me a 30-minute quick primer on tail-call optimization. Do not split it into multiple pages.
evals.expected_output: Quick-primer mode: one index.html file with h2 sections, concept map, at least one scenario worked example, and inline self-check. It does not create separate chapter files. A primer still includes retrieval practice and at least three figures.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: either a forced multi-file scaffold or a prose summary with no concept map and no self-check.

evals.name: one-shot-primer-no-interview
evals.prompt: Give me a primer on Redux.
evals.expected_output: A minimal one-line request should not trigger a five-question interview. The skill should make defensible assumptions, produce a primer-depth concept-focused tutorial, and document assumptions near the top of index.html.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: five scope questions that block a user who clearly asked for a primer.

evals.name: diataxis-route-away-non-learning
evals.prompt: This Python code raises KeyError. Can you help me find the bug?
evals.expected_output: This is work-oriented debugging intent, not learning intent. The skill should route away: use debugging, or ask whether the user wants the code fixed or wants to learn the underlying mechanism. It should not produce a full tutorial.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: a multi-chapter tutorial generated for a one-off debugging request.

evals.name: explicit-non-english-output
evals.prompt: Write the LLM inference acceleration tutorial in Chinese, but keep community English terms such as speculative decoding, continuous batching, chunked prefill, and KV cache.
evals.expected_output: The tutorial honors the explicitly requested output language while keeping the same structure and verification intent. Visible headings may be Chinese, but structural sections keep stable data-tech-tutorial markers so gates remain language-independent. It preserves standard community English terms for unsettled vocabulary, gives first-use plain-language glosses, does not invent translated labels, and includes dated frontier framing because the domain is moving quickly.
evals.baseline: Without this skill: either ignores the requested language because the skill is English-first, or hard-translates emerging terms into invented local labels with no community usage.

evals.name: route-single-article-to-explain-article
evals.prompt: Write an article explaining why PKCE exists in OAuth 2.0.
evals.expected_output: A single explanatory article about one mechanism is explain-article's job. The skill should not trigger, or should hand off to explain-article, and must not produce a multi-chapter tutorial.
evals.baseline: Without the boundary: a multi-chapter HTML tutorial for a request that asked for one article.

evals.name: route-single-diagram-to-visual-explainer
evals.prompt: 画一张图解释 TCP 三次握手。
evals.expected_output: One standalone diagram is visual-explainer's job. The skill should not trigger, or should hand off to visual-explainer, and must not produce a tutorial.
evals.baseline: Without the boundary: a tutorial site built around a request for one diagram.

evals.name: chinese-learning-trigger
evals.prompt: 我想系统学习 Rust 的所有权和借用，给我写一套教程，用中文。
evals.expected_output: A Chinese learning request triggers the skill. It produces a multi-file tutorial in Chinese with <html lang> set to zh, keeps data-tech-tutorial markers, and keeps standard Rust terms (ownership, borrow checker, lifetime).
evals.baseline: Without Chinese triggers: the request is not routed to this skill, or the output ignores the requested language.

evals.name: chinese-ste-inspired-conceptual-learning
evals.prompt: 用中文写一个单页 HTML 教程，教一个有 Python 基础、刚接触并发的读者理解互斥锁。借鉴 ASD-STE100，让句子直接、结构清楚。保留互斥锁、临界区、竞争条件这些已有术语。核心例子是：两个线程分别读取同一个计数器的旧值，各自加一，再写回；如果两个线程都先读到 0，最后可能只得到 1。解释互斥锁怎样让使用同一把锁的线程依次进入临界区，也说明进程内的一把锁不会自动协调多个服务进程。不要写成 API 名词清单。
evals.expected_output: A Chinese conceptual primer teaches the concrete interleaving before or alongside the mechanism. It connects the shared read-modify-write sequence to the lost update, then explains how the same mutex serializes participating threads and where that guarantee stops. Established Chinese terms stay stable and receive plain explanations. STE is identified, if discussed, as an inspiration for Chinese writing; no formal Chinese compliance or invented character ceiling is claimed.
evals.baseline: Expected failure modes, not a measured baseline: a rigid Chinese character cap, an unsupported STE-compliance claim, euphemisms replacing established terms, or a short explanation that omits the same-lock or process boundary.

grading_rubric.pass: The reader can trace a specific lost-update schedule, explain the mutex's role, and identify the same-lock and process limits in clear Chinese.
fail_if: The result is presented as always 1, or the explanation attributes the lost update to the mutex.
The tutorial implies that a mutex coordinates code that does not use it or automatically coordinates separate service processes.
The author claims Chinese ASD-STE100 compliance or imposes a fixed Chinese character limit as an STE requirement.

evals.name: concise-tutorial-rewrite-preserves-source-semantics
evals.prompt: Replace the operational-behavior paragraph in my fictional Relay v2 tutorial. Make it short and decisive; prefer direct wording and remove any unnecessary hedging. I need the replacement paragraph now, without a scope interview or a full new tutorial. Source: Only after the operator approves the maintenance window may the controller restart the worker. Approval permits a restart; it does not require one. During a restart, the controller records events while the monitor checks worker health; these actions run concurrently. In v2, enabling the cache may reduce repeated reads, but the benefit depends on the cache hit rate. This procedure has not been verified for v3.
evals.expected_output: A concise replacement preserves the source's facts despite the pressure for decisive language: operator approval is a prerequisite, restarting remains optional, recording and health checking remain concurrent, cache benefit is conditional on hit rate and scoped to v2, and v3 remains unverified. The output does not turn permissions or predictions into commands or guarantees.
evals.baseline: Expected failure modes, not a measured baseline: changing may to must or will, dropping the only-after condition, making parallel actions sequential, promising cache improvement, or extending the procedure to unverified v3.

grading_rubric.pass: All five invariants survive: prior approval, optional restart, concurrent actions, conditional v2 cache benefit, and unverified v3. Concision is judged only after semantic preservation.
fail_if: Restarting becomes mandatory after approval, is allowed before approval, or the operator's role disappears.
Recording is described as occurring before or after health checking instead of concurrently.
The cache is guaranteed to reduce reads, its hit-rate condition or v2 scope disappears, or v3 is described as supported or tested.

evals.name: english-local-hands-on-observable-procedure
evals.prompt: Write a single-file English hands-on tutorial called PulseLab that teaches a Python beginner how the working directory affects relative input and output paths. Use only Bash and Python 3.11+ standard-library commands. The shell may initially be in any directory. Create a fresh local pulse-lab directory with config/input.json containing {"service":"pulse","enabled":true}, then use python3 -m json.tool config/input.json formatted.json to create readable JSON in formatted.json. Explain what the learner should observe and how to diagnose a missing-input-path error. Do not execute the commands in this evaluation; provide the tutorial only.
evals.expected_output: The tutorial states the supplied environment assumptions, establishes and identifies a writable lab directory, creates the required JSON input, and makes each relative path's base clear. Material steps include observable checkpoints: directory and input existence, successful formatting, and inspecting formatted.json. A wrong-path check helps the learner distinguish an incorrect working directory from a missing input file. All command outcomes are labeled as expected because execution was explicitly excluded.
evals.baseline: Expected failure modes, not a measured baseline: commands assume an unstated working directory, the input file or setup is missing, expected output is confused with stdout when the formatter writes a file, or unexecuted results are reported as observed success.

grading_rubric.pass: A reader starting in another directory can establish the lab, create valid input, run the formatter from the stated location, inspect its file output, and diagnose the supplied path error without guessing.
fail_if: Setup does not establish the current directory or fails to create config/input.json before it is used.
The tutorial claims the successful formatter invocation prints the formatted JSON to stdout despite the output-file argument, or gives no way to inspect formatted.json.
The wrong-path advice has no concrete directory or file check, or the delivery claims that commands or checks were executed.

evals.name: reader-level-simplification-retains-technical-meaning
evals.prompt: For a hash-table tutorial, draft two short versions of the same teaching section: one for a novice programmer and one for an engineer who already implements data structures. Use clear professional English and STE-inspired writing where useful. Work from this supplied model rather than researching a different implementation: a hash function chooses a bucket; separate chaining stores colliding entries in that bucket; lookup traverses that bucket. With a suitable hash function and a bounded load factor, expected lookup is O(1), but worst-case lookup is O(n). Resizing rehashes entries and can cost O(n) for one operation; expected amortized insertion can still be O(1). This is not a bound on every operation's latency. Make the novice version easy to follow and the expert version direct.
evals.expected_output: Both versions preserve the supplied hash-to-bucket and chaining mechanism and distinguish expected, worst-case, and amortized claims. The novice version explains established terms through a concrete worked situation; the expert version reaches assumptions, costs, and the latency boundary promptly. Necessary terms such as separate chaining, load factor, and amortized remain available and consistent rather than being removed through a dictionary ban or replaced with coined labels.
evals.baseline: Expected failure modes, not a measured baseline: a novice slogan that hash tables are always O(1), omission of a resize cost or latency boundary, identical scaffolding for both audiences, or removal of necessary technical terms to imitate a controlled-language dictionary.

grading_rubric.pass: The versions differ in scaffolding while preserving the mechanism, hash/load assumptions, expected versus worst-case lookup, single-resize cost, and amortized versus per-operation latency distinction.
fail_if: Either version converts an expected or amortized bound into a guarantee for every operation.
Either version omits the bucket traversal mechanism, suitability/load-factor assumptions, or the resize and latency boundary.
The novice gets unexplained jargon with no concrete worked situation, the expert gets the same novice scaffolding, or necessary terms are rejected solely as non-dictionary words.
